prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1, its active form and its physiological actions, which made possible incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-achievement prize for B031 to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. After reading all six round-1 statements I tested the case again without leaning on the opening count. The scientific chain is intact at every step: proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide, the human physiology of secretion and action, receptor and proglucagon-derived peptide biology, then durable receptor agonism whose effects on glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal outcomes have been confirmed by independent randomized trials. It is originality plus maturity plus breadth, and recognition is timely and arguably overdue. I have changed the citation, not the names. Following Wahren-Herlenius, the wording now names the active form and the therapies it enabled, so that leaving out Knudsen is not read as a verdict that the drugs were unimportant while the prize still rewards the discovery chain that every member regards as the core.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness, and I will not paper over it. Mojsov's priority for identifying the active peptide relative to the Habener group, who are not on the credited list, cannot be settled from the supplied evidence, and I have only recollection of the historical record. Excluding Knudsen leaves the long-acting analogue design outside the credit, and a reader could take the prize as honouring physiology while skipping the medicine. Long-term safety, durability of weight loss and the central mechanisms of weight reduction are still being characterised, which could change how the achievement is later described. The three-person cap also means a second part cannot be added without cutting inside the GLP-1 trio.

responses.point: Moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio, asks that the citation name the therapies that followed, and insists that Mojsov's priority claim not be treated as settled because we all rely on recollection.
responses.response: I accept both points and have rewritten the citation to name the active form and the incretin-based therapies it enabled. On priority, you are right that agreement among us is not evidence. The supplied record documents Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and I credit within the names supplied, but I cannot show that her claim outranks Habener's. My rule is therefore explicit: if any member can show from the supplied evidence that her claim does not hold, the third slot should go to Knudsen, and I would want that raised before the vote. Absent that, I keep Mojsov, because a discovery prize should place the identification of the peptide ahead of analogue engineering that rests on it. I also take your reminder that anti-TNF is as clean a bench-to-bedside story as any, but I still hold it for a later year.

responses.point: Presses whether omitting Knudsen is defensible at the final ballot, since the citation must then be written around discovery of the hormone and its actions rather than the drugs, and holds the unfolded protein response as the fall-back if the credit split cannot be defended.
responses.response: It is defensible if the citation is honest about what is being rewarded, and that is the reason for the new wording. The prize recognises the discovery of the hormone, its active form and its actions, and states that therapies followed; it does not claim to credit their engineering. On the unfolded protein response, I still see the pair of Walter and Mori as compact and the concept as original, but your own round-1 case concedes narrower disease impact and early translation, and the mammalian PERK and ATF6 branches sit outside the credit. I do not see a concrete clinical anchor that would make it a better fall-back than a GLP-1 trio whose only flaw is one contested name. If the Mojsov claim collapsed, I would swap in Knudsen before abandoning GLP-1 for B042.

responses.point: Argues that if a second part is wanted, CAR-T is preferable to the other options on clinical impact, that Eshhar's concept is outside the credit, and that the committee, not a displaced name, should decide whether drug development is honoured in a separate part.
responses.response: I agree that CAR-T is the strongest second candidate on clinical impact, but I do not support a second part this year. The cap of three people means a second part would force out one of the GLP-1 trio, which weakens a prize whose discovery chain is strong and complete. For CAR-T specifically, Eshhar's chimeric-receptor concept is outside the credit and Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is less tied to CAR engineering than the work of June and Sadelain, so a trio would not match the history. I keep it as my first alternative, not as a pairing. Your suggestion that drug development should be honoured, if at all, as a separate part is the right framing, but with a three-person cap it argues for a different year, not for diluting this one.

responses.point: Disagrees with replacing Mojsov by Knudsen, saying drug design should be debated as an explicit choice, and describes channelrhodopsin work as a genuine discovery about a light-gated channel but with emerging medical impact.
responses.response: I agree that substituting Knudsen for Mojsov must be an explicit committee decision and not something that falls out of a priority dispute, and I want the vote to reflect that choice. My position is that the discovery chain takes precedence in a prize of this kind. On optogenetics, I accept your point that channelrhodopsin characterisation is a discovery about a channel and not only a tool, and I no longer rely on a tool-versus-discovery distinction against B019. The weight against it this year is the six credited names for three places and clinical translation that is only starting, not the status of the work. We differ slightly on whether the clinical gap is decisive, but we agree it does not outrank GLP-1.

responses.point: Treats Knudsen as an alternative third slot, would move to her if Mojsov's priority claim fails, and argues the tradition of the prize is strongest on the discovery side.
responses.response: We agree on the structure of the decision: Mojsov stays unless the record shows her claim fails, and then Knudsen takes the third place. I would add that the cost of the alternative is not zero. A Knudsen trio moves the prize toward industrial development and away from the physiology of Holst and Drucker, which is the part of the story that is broadest in biology, including the gut-to-brain appetite axis you mention. I do not accept familiarity with a method as a reason to raise optogenetics. I note your caution on TOR and your reading that my fourth-place ranking pushes it too far, and I have not moved it into my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide holds against the Habener group; I rely on recollection and the supplied evidence cannot settle it.
Whether the committee prefers to credit the discovery chain or to include drug development through Knudsen, which determines the third name and the citation.
Whether long-term safety, durability of weight loss and newer indications will change how the achievement should be described.
Whether a two-part configuration is better than a single GLP-1 prize, given that any second achievement forces a cut within the trio.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my profile. I worked with Paul Greengard during my postdoctoral period and have about twenty documented co-authored works with fellow committee member Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy. None involves a shortlisted name. I declare that neuroscience colleagues in the optogenetics field are close to my area, though I have no documented tie to any of the six credited optogenetics names. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure. As chair I should not press my own ranking beyond what the evidence supports.
